prompt: Why does the course recommend an Ubuntu 24.04 virtual machine even to somebody whose Mac can install a JDK and Maven directly?
hint: What does a difference between your screen and the page then tell you?

choices.text: Maven does not run on macOS
choices.why: It does; maven.apache.org and Homebrew both install it there. The section names that path as a real option.

choices.text: It is the system the transcripts were recorded on
choices.why: Right. When your screen and a transcript disagree, the difference is then in what you typed, not in the Maven or the system underneath.

choices.text: A build inside a virtual machine runs faster than on the computer that hosts it
choices.why: A simulated computer shares the real one's processors and memory; it is never the faster of the two.

choices.text: Java 25 is only published for Linux
choices.why: OpenJDK builds exist for macOS and Windows too; Eclipse Temurin is one the section names.

prompt: The JDK and Maven take about 400 MB. Why does the course still ask for a virtual machine with 4 GB of memory and a 30 GB disk?

choices.text: Maven keeps every library it downloads in memory between builds
choices.why: Maven is a new process on every run and keeps nothing in memory; the libraries live on disk, in ~/.m2.

choices.text: Ubuntu Server alone needs 4 GB to boot
choices.why: The server edition is the light one; the memory is for what this course runs on it.

choices.text: Later lessons run an app, a database and Docker at once
choices.why: Right. Lesson 9 adds the database and lesson 19 Docker with its images, and a test run starts all of them at once.

choices.text: The hypervisor reserves half of the machine for itself
choices.why: A hypervisor needs some memory of its own on the host, outside the virtual machine; it does not take a share of the 4 GB you give the guest.

prompt: What is `~/.mavenrc`?

choices.text: Options mvn reads before it starts Java
choices.why: Right. That is why one line there reaches every Maven run and nothing else.

choices.text: The project file where dependencies are declared
choices.why: That is pom.xml, inside each project. ~/.mavenrc is in your home and belongs to no project.

choices.text: The directory where downloaded libraries are kept
choices.why: That is ~/.m2/repository, a directory. ~/.mavenrc is a one-line file.

choices.text: A setting that every java command on the machine reads
choices.why: Only the mvn script reads it. A program started with java never sees it.

prompt: The four `sun.misc.Unsafe` warnings appear before the project has a single class. Whose code triggers them?

choices.text: Commons Validator, the project's dependency
choices.why: They appear with no project at all, on mvn -v, before any dependency is read.

choices.text: The JDK's own launcher
choices.why: The JDK prints the warning, but it names the caller, and the caller is a library inside Maven.

choices.text: Guava, inside Maven itself
choices.why: Right. It is Maven's code calling a part of the JDK that Java 25 is retiring, which is why a line for Maven alone is the fix.

choices.text: Ubuntu's packaging scripts
choices.why: apt ran once at install time; these lines come from the running JVM every time mvn starts.

prompt: `java -version` says 25, and `mvn -v` says `Java version: 21`. Which JDK will compile the project when you run `mvn package`?
hint: Maven decides before your pom is read.

choices.text: 25, because it is the one on the path
choices.why: The path is only Maven's second choice; JAVA_HOME, when set, comes first.

choices.text: 21, the one mvn -v reports
choices.why: Right. mvn -v says what Maven will start, which is why it is the line to read when two JDKs are installed.

choices.text: Whichever is newer, since Maven picks the newest JDK installed
choices.why: Maven does not search for JDKs; it takes JAVA_HOME or the java on the path, whatever its version.

choices.text: The one named in maven.compiler.release
choices.why: That property tells the compiler which Java to produce code for; it does not choose which JDK runs.

prompt: Which of these does `mvn -v` tell you? Choose every one that applies.

choices.text: The JDK that will run the build
choices.why: Right: the Java version and runtime lines.

choices.text: Where Maven itself is installed
choices.why: Right: Maven home, /usr/share/maven for Ubuntu's package.

choices.text: The plugin versions your project's build will use
choices.why: mvn -v reads no pom; plugin versions only appear when a project is built.

choices.text: The encoding the JDK would read files with by default
choices.why: Right: platform encoding, the default a pom overrides with project.build.sourceEncoding.

choices.text: Whether javac is installed
choices.why: mvn -v starts the java launcher only; javac -version is the command that answers that.

prompt: On a machine where `java -version` works, `javac -version` answers `command not found`. What was installed?

choices.text: Nothing: Java is missing
choices.why: java answered, so a Java is there. What is missing is narrower.

choices.text: Maven without its compiler plugin
choices.why: javac is a command of the JDK, not of Maven; Maven's plugins call it, they do not provide it.

choices.text: A JDK older than 25
choices.why: An older JDK still has javac, and javac -version would print its version.

choices.text: A Java runtime package instead of openjdk-25-jdk
choices.why: Right. A runtime runs programs and has no compiler; the JDK package adds javac.

prompt: Right after adding the line to `~/.mavenrc`, `mvn -v` prints `Unrecognized option: --sun-misc-unsafe-memory-access=allow` and nothing else from Maven. What is the first thing to check?

choices.text: Whether the line was typed with the wrong quotes
choices.why: A wrong quote breaks the shell script that reads the file, with a shell error; this message comes from a JVM that read the flag correctly and did not know it.

choices.text: Which JDK mvn starts, through JAVA_HOME
choices.why: Right. JDK 21 does not know the flag and refuses to start; echo $JAVA_HOME and update-java-alternatives -l say which JDK it is.

choices.text: Whether Maven 3.8.7 is too old for the flag
choices.why: Maven only passes the flag on; the program refusing it is the java launcher.

choices.text: Whether the project's pom asks for Java 25
choices.why: mvn -v reads no pom, and the JVM failed before any project was looked at.

prompt: With no configuration at all, Maven compiles the JUnit classes of a project from `src/___/java`.
Two projects in different companies both declare `groupId` `com.example`, `artifactId` `isbn-check` and `version` `1.0.0`. What follows?

choices.text: Nothing: Maven tells them apart by the directory they are built in
choices.why: A repository has no idea where a jar was built; it files it by the three coordinates and nothing else.

choices.text: Maven refuses to build the second one
choices.why: Maven builds either happily. The clash only shows when both reach the same repository.

choices.text: One overwrites the other in a repository
choices.why: Right. The coordinates are the address, which is why a real group id is a domain its owner controls.

choices.text: The packaging element decides which one wins
choices.why: packaging says what the build produces; it is not part of what names the project.

prompt: What does `<maven.compiler.release>25</maven.compiler.release>` change?

choices.text: javac targets and checks against Java 25
choices.why: Right. It is a setting for the compiler plugin, written as a property.

choices.text: Maven downloads and uses a JDK 25 if the machine has another
choices.why: Maven 3.8.7 downloads no JDK; it compiles with the one it was started on, and that one has to know release 25.

choices.text: The version of the project itself
choices.why: That is the version element, 1.0.0. The property is about Java, not about your project.

choices.text: Which version of maven-compiler-plugin runs
choices.why: The plugin version is pinned in pluginManagement; this property is read by whichever version runs, if it knows it.

prompt: The pom names two dependencies, and `dependency:tree` lists many more. Where did the others come from?

choices.text: Maven adds a standard set to every project
choices.why: A project with no dependencies has an empty tree; nothing is added by default.

choices.text: From the poms of the two dependencies, and of theirs in turn
choices.why: Right. Each library's pom declares what it needs, and Maven follows those all the way down.

choices.text: From the plugins that ran during the build
choices.why: Plugins have dependencies of their own, but those never appear in your project's tree.

choices.text: From the imports in the Java sources
choices.why: Maven never reads your imports; a library the code imports and the pom omits fails to compile.

prompt: Match each scope to where its dependency is visible.

pairs.right: the program, its tests, and when it runs
compiling, but supplied by where it runs
running, but never compiling the program

prompt: Your pom declares library A, which needs X 2.0. It also declares B, which needs C, which needs X 3.0. Nothing else mentions X. Which X does the build use?
hint: Count the steps from your pom to each X.

choices.why: Right. It is two steps from your project and 3.0 is three; nearest wins, whichever is newer.

choices.text: X 3.0, because the newest version wins
choices.why: That is the rule people expect and not Maven's. Maven chooses by distance in the graph.

choices.text: Both, one for A and one for C
choices.why: A Java classpath holds one copy of a class; Maven puts exactly one version of X on it.

choices.text: Neither: the build stops with a conflict error
choices.why: Maven resolves the conflict silently; only -Dverbose on the tree shows the loser.

prompt: A transitive library arrives at a version with a known bug, and you need a newer one. What is the direct way to get it?

choices.text: Delete its directory from ~/.m2/repository
choices.why: Maven downloads the same version again on the next build; the pom decides which version, not the cache.

choices.text: Add an exclusion for it to the dependency that brings it
choices.why: An exclusion removes it, and then no version is there at all for the code that needs it.

choices.text: Declare it in your own pom at the version you want
choices.why: Right. Your own declaration is the nearest there is, so it wins over every transitive one.

choices.text: Run mvn with -U to update every dependency
choices.why: -U refreshes snapshot and metadata checks; it never changes a version the graph has already chosen.

prompt: Put these phases of the default lifecycle in the order `mvn install` runs them.
What does `mvn package` run?

choices.text: The jar plugin, and nothing else
choices.why: Naming a phase never runs it alone; the jar would have no classes in it.

choices.text: Every phase up to package, with their goals
choices.why: Right. Compiling and testing come along because they are earlier phases.

choices.text: A script stored in the pom under the name package
choices.why: A pom holds no scripts; the phases and their order are Maven's, the same in every project.

choices.text: Every phase including install and deploy
choices.why: The phases after the one you name do not run; package stops at package.

prompt: You typed `mvn dependency:tree`. Which phases of the default lifecycle ran?

choices.text: All of them up to compile, because the tree needs compiled classes
choices.why: The tree is read from poms, not from classes, and nothing was compiled.

choices.text: validate only, the first phase
choices.why: No phase was named, so not even validate ran.

choices.text: None: a goal named directly runs alone
choices.why: Right. plugin:goal runs that one goal and no phase at all.

choices.text: The phase the dependency plugin is bound to
choices.why: It is bound to none, which is why naming its goal is the only way it runs.

prompt: Another project on the same machine wants to use `com.example:isbn-check:1.0.0` as a dependency. Which command makes that possible?

choices.text: mvn package, because it builds the jar
choices.why: The jar it builds stays in target/, where no other project looks.

choices.text: mvn deploy
choices.why: deploy uploads to a shared remote repository, which needs a server this course does not set up; it is more than the question asks.

choices.text: mvn verify
choices.why: verify ends where package ends, plus checks; nothing leaves target/.

choices.text: mvn install
choices.why: Right. It copies the jar and its pom into ~/.m2/repository, where every build on the machine resolves dependencies.

prompt: In the `mvn package` run of this lesson, how many plugin goals ran, counting each `---` line once?
With the `<build>` element deleted, `mvn clean package` failed with `Source option 5 is no longer supported`, although the pom still says `<maven.compiler.release>25</maven.compiler.release>`. Why?

choices.text: Deleting <build> also deleted the properties
choices.why: The sed range ran from <build> to </build>; the properties block sits above it and was untouched.

choices.text: The default compiler plugin 3.1 ignores it
choices.why: Right. 3.1 is older than the release setting and fell back on its own default of Java 5.

choices.text: Without <build> Maven runs the build with the oldest JDK installed
choices.why: The JDK is chosen before the pom is read, from JAVA_HOME or the path; it was still 25.

choices.text: JDK 25 cannot compile code that has no build section
choices.why: javac knows nothing of poms; it was handed -source 5 by the old plugin, and that is what it refused.

prompt: A plugin is declared under `<pluginManagement>` and named nowhere else in the pom. What does that declaration do?

choices.text: It runs the plugin's default goal in every build
choices.why: pluginManagement runs nothing; a goal runs because a phase binds it or because you name it.

choices.text: Nothing, until the plugin is also listed under <plugins>
choices.why: The dependency plugin was listed only there and still answered dependency:tree at 3.11.0.

choices.text: It fixes the version whenever the plugin runs
choices.why: Right. That is why one block pins both the lifecycle plugins and the dependency plugin.

choices.text: It downloads the plugin into the project's target directory
choices.why: Plugins go to ~/.m2/repository like any other artifact, and only when a build needs them.

prompt: `java -cp target/isbn-check-1.0.0.jar com.example.isbn.IsbnCheck ...` ends in `NoClassDefFoundError` for `ISBNValidator`, although `mvn package` passed. Why?

choices.text: The compile scope is only for compiling, not for running
choices.why: compile scope is needed when the program runs too; the classpath simply did not name the jar.

choices.text: mvn package left the library out because the tests did not need it
choices.why: The tests did use it, through the program. Maven never puts dependencies in this jar at all.

choices.text: The jar holds only our own classes
choices.why: Right. jar tf showed one class of ours; the library sits in ~/.m2 until the classpath names it.

choices.text: The class was compiled for Java 25 and the JVM is older
choices.why: An older JVM fails with UnsupportedClassVersionError, on our own class, before it looks for any library.

prompt: A colleague's build of the same project passes on Maven 3.9 and fails on your Maven 3.8.7 at the compiler. Their pom has no `<build>` element. What is the most likely cause?

choices.text: Your JDK is older than hers
choices.why: Possible in general, but mvn -v would show it, and an older JDK fails with "release version 25 not supported", not at the plugin's choice of version.

choices.text: Maven 3.8.7 cannot build Java 25 projects
choices.why: It built this lesson's project once the plugins were pinned.

choices.text: Each Maven picks its own unpinned compiler plugin
choices.why: Right. Hers picks a newer one that reads maven.compiler.release; yours picks 3.1, which does not. A pin makes both build alike.

choices.text: Her local repository holds a newer copy of Commons Validator
choices.why: A dependency's version is the pom's, the same on both machines; the cache only holds what the pom named.

prompt: Which of these make a Maven build of this project mean the same on every machine? Choose every one that applies.

choices.text: Every plugin the build uses has its version written in pluginManagement
choices.why: Right. Otherwise each Maven installation picks its own, as the detour showed.

choices.text: Every dependency in the pom has an exact version
choices.why: Right. The coordinates then name one file in Central for everybody.

choices.text: The pom names the source encoding instead of trusting the platform default
choices.why: Right. A machine set to another encoding would otherwise read the same sources differently.

choices.text: Everybody runs mvn clean before every build
choices.why: clean empties target/; it does not change which versions of anything are used.

choices.text: The project's jars are copied into the project directory
choices.why: Maven keeps them in ~/.m2, and the coordinates already decide which ones; copying them only adds a second place to be wrong.

prompt: On a new machine with an empty `~/.m2`, you run `mvn package` in this lesson's project. Put what happens in order.
items: missing plugins and dependencies are downloaded into ~/.m2

prompt: After the detour, a build log ends in `Tests run: 0` and `BUILD SUCCESS` for a project whose `src/test/java` holds three tests. What does that log establish?

choices.text: That the three tests pass
choices.why: None of them ran, so the log says nothing about whether they pass.

choices.text: Only that the code compiled and a jar was written
choices.why: Right. The test phase ran, its plugin found nothing it could execute, and success is all a run of nothing can report.

choices.text: That the tests were skipped on purpose with -DskipTests
choices.why: Nobody passed that flag; a skipped run says "Tests are skipped" instead.

choices.text: That the test classes failed to compile
choices.why: A compile error stops the build with BUILD FAILURE before the test phase is reached.
